slides.text:
A cobra command can run inside a program, with no terminal: you give it arguments, catch what it prints and read the error it returns.

That is all a test of a CLI needs. You will build it step by step, in plain programs that print a result.

A real test lives in a `_test.go` file. Here the single `main.go` editor stands in for it: each program runs the command and prints the result.

Three sessions:

- **Session 1:** run a command in memory and test a flag
- **Session 2:** several cases, errors and bad arguments
- **Session 3:** subcommands, input and help text

A test drives a command the way a user would, but in memory. The output goes to a buffer and the arguments come from a list.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
cmd = build the command
output -> a buffer
args -> ["greet", "--name", "Ana"]
run cmd
compare the buffer to the expected text

exercises.title: Run a command in memory
exercises.guide: Build a command, run it in code and read what it printed.

chunks.guide: A function that builds the command. It writes to the command's own output, not straight to the terminal.

notes.text: The writer a test can swap for a buffer

chunks.guide: Collect the output in a buffer and give the command its arguments.

notes.text: Sends the command's output into the buffer
The arguments to run with, so os.Args is never read

chunks.text:
cmd := newGreetCmd()
    buf := new(bytes.Buffer)
    cmd.SetOut(buf)
    cmd.SetArgs([]string{})

chunks.guide: Run the command, then print what the buffer caught.
chunks.text:
cmd.Execute()
    fmt.Print(buf.String())

exercises.title: A run helper
exercises.guide: Wrap the three steps in a function every test can call.

chunks.guide: The command and the imports are already in the file. The helper returns the output and the error.

notes.text: A test needs both the text and the failure

chunks.text:
func run(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) (string, error) {
    buf := new(bytes.Buffer)
    cmd.SetOut(buf)
    cmd.SetArgs(args)
    err := cmd.Execute()
    return buf.String(), err
}

chunks.guide: Call the helper with a fresh command.
chunks.text:
out, err := run(newGreetCmd(), []string{})
    fmt.Print(out)
    fmt.Println("error:", err)

exercises.title: Prepare the command
exercises.guide: Send the output to the buffer, then give the command the arguments to run with.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `fmt.Println` writes straight to the terminal, so `SetOut` never sees it and the buffer stays empty. Writing to `cmd.OutOrStdout()` is what lets a test catch the text.

exercises.title: Test a flag
exercises.guide: Pass a flag through the arguments and check the output.

chunks.guide: The imports and the helper are already in the file. The command greets whoever `--name` says.
Flags go in the argument list, as on a real command line.
chunks.text:
out, _ := run(newGreetCmd(), []string{"--name", "Ana"})
    fmt.Print(out)

chunks.guide: With no flag, the default shows.
chunks.text:
out, _ = run(newGreetCmd(), []string{})
    fmt.Print(out)

slides.text: `Execute` returns the error instead of exiting. Only `main` turns an error into an exit code, so a test can read the error and move on.

Cobra can print an error and the usage by itself. A test usually silences both and checks the returned error, the way a user of the command never would.

To catch that text instead, `SetErr` sends the command's error output to a buffer, as `SetOut` does for the normal output.

exercises.title: A table of cases
exercises.guide: Check several runs with one loop, each on a fresh command.

chunks.guide: The command, the flag and the helper are in the file. List the arguments and the output each run should give.
Run every case and compare. The command is built inside the loop.

notes.text: A new command per case, so no flag value carries over

exercises.title: Test a failing command
exercises.guide: Make the command fail and check the error that Execute returns.

chunks.guide: The helper is already in the file. The command always fails with an error.

notes.text: Stops cobra printing the usage after an error
Stops cobra printing the error, so the test reads it

chunks.guide: A failing run returns the error and prints nothing to the buffer.
chunks.text:
out, err := run(newGreetCmd(), []string{})
    fmt.Printf("out=%q\n", out)
    fmt.Println("err:", err)

exercises.title: Test the arguments check
exercises.guide: Run a command with the wrong number of arguments, then the right one.

chunks.guide: The helper is already in the file. The command wants exactly one argument.
Too few arguments: the error comes from cobra, before the command runs.
chunks.text:
_, err := run(newGreetCmd(), []string{})
    fmt.Println(err)

chunks.guide: With one argument the command runs.
chunks.text:
out, err := run(newGreetCmd(), []string{"Ana"})
    fmt.Print(out)
    fmt.Println(err)

exercises.title: Guard the arguments
exercises.guide: Require exactly one argument, and keep cobra from printing the usage when it fails.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: The command declares no `--verbose` flag, so parsing fails and `Execute` returns the parse error. The `Error:` prefix is added only when cobra prints the error itself, and that is silenced.

slides.text:
A real test goes through the root command, with the arguments a user types, and can also feed it input and ask for its help.

A command keeps its own state: flags, arguments and buffers. Think about how you build the ones a test uses.

exercises.title: Test a subcommand
exercises.guide: Reach a subcommand the way a user does, through the root command.

chunks.guide: The subcommand and the helper are already in the file. A function builds the whole tree, fresh every call.

notes.text: Attaches greet, so the arguments can name it

chunks.guide: The first argument picks the subcommand.
chunks.text:
out, err := run(newRootCmd(), []string{"greet"})
    fmt.Print(out)
    fmt.Println("error:", err)

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: `newGreetCmd` has a `--name` flag that defaults to `world`. Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
func main() {
    cmd := newGreetCmd()

    out, _ := run(cmd, []string{"--name", "Ana"})
    fmt.Print(out)

    out, _ = run(cmd, []string{})
    fmt.Print(out)
}
exercises.explanation: Flag values live inside the command and nothing resets them. The second run parses no flags, so `name` keeps the "Ana" the first run set. A fresh command per run avoids it.

exercises.title: Feed the command input
exercises.guide: Give a command that reads input some text, with no keyboard.

chunks.guide: The helper is already in the file. The command reads one line, from its own input.

notes.text: The input the command reads, so a test can replace it

chunks.guide: Replace the keyboard with a reader.

notes.text: Feeds the command this text as its input

chunks.text:
cmd := newAskCmd()
    cmd.SetIn(strings.NewReader("Ana\n"))

chunks.guide: Run it as before.
chunks.text:
out, _ := run(cmd, []string{})
    fmt.Print(out)

exercises.title: Replace the input
exercises.guide: Give the command the reader as its input.

exercises.title: Test the help
exercises.guide: Ask for help and check that the output holds what you expect.

chunks.guide: The command, with a short description, and the helper are in the file. Ask for help like a user.

notes.text: Cobra adds this flag itself and prints to the output

chunks.text:
out, err := run(newGreetCmd(), []string{"--help"})
    fmt.Println(err)

chunks.guide: Check for pieces of the text, not all of it.
chunks.text:
fmt.Println(strings.Contains(out, "Usage:"))
    fmt.Println(strings.Contains(out, "Say hello"))

exercises.title: Why a function?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick what it is for.
options: Registers the command once for the whole program
Runs the command and returns its output
Builds a fresh command, so each test starts clean
exercises.explanation: Every call returns a new command with its own flags and subcommands, so no test inherits the state of another. A package-level variable would be shared by all of them.
